analysis.one_liner: Gives college athletes federal collective bargaining rights as employees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote: it was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced in December 2023 and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025, despite 10 Democratic sponsors and cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act so that college athletes who receive scholarships or other direct compensation are treated as employees with the legal right to form unions. They could then bargain collectively with their colleges and their athletic conferences over pay, health and safety, and working conditions. The bill allows unions to organize across rival schools within a conference, since no single college has enough power to negotiate with a whole league, and it bars athletes from being forced to sign away these rights. It also states that none of this changes how scholarships are taxed or how athletes qualify for federal financial aid.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly half a million college athletes who play for schools in big-money conferences, plus athletes at smaller schools who could follow. They would gain the same legal protections private-sector workers have: the right to organize, join a union, and negotiate over compensation, hours, and safety instead of accepting terms set unilaterally by their schools and the NCAA. The bill's own findings note that intercollegiate sports generate more than $15 billion a year in revenue while athletes are compensated only in scholarships and stipends [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Scholarship college athletes in revenue sports

how_it_helps.text: College athletes receiving any direct compensation, including scholarships whose terms require playing a sport, would be counted as employees under the National Labor Relations Act, giving them the right to organize and bargain collectively [S2].
The bill extends the National Labor Relations Board's authority to public universities, which the law normally does not cover, so athletes at state schools could unionize too [S2].

Athletes could form bargaining units that span multiple rival schools within a conference, with the schools treated as a single multiemployer unit, so that bargaining happens at the level where the rules actually get made [S2].
No athlete could be required to sign an agreement, including a scholarship agreement or legal settlement, that waives the rights this bill creates [S2].
The bill explicitly leaves tax treatment of scholarships and eligibility for federal financial aid untouched, so unionization would not create a new tax bill for athletes or endanger their aid [S2].

analysis.who_pays: College athletic departments and the athletic conferences that currently set compensation and playing rules without bargaining. Schools would have to negotiate pay and conditions with athlete unions, and collectively bargained compensation would come out of athletic revenues. The NCAA itself is carved out of the bill's definition of a bargaining counterparty, so universities and conferences, not the association, would sit across the table [S2].

drawbacks.text: Critics of treating athletes as employees argue it could strain the finances of athletic programs outside the wealthy football and basketball powerhouses, potentially forcing cuts to non-revenue sports such as swimming, tennis, and track that do not generate income. The bill does not exempt smaller schools from the definition of employer [S2].

Collectively bargaining pay across rival schools within a conference would be an unusual structure, and the bill excludes the NCAA from the bargaining table even though it sets many of the rules athletes live under, which limits how much of the system the unions could actually change [S2].

Some defenders of the traditional amateur model argue that athlete pay negotiated by unions could widen the gap between big-revenue programs and everyone else, and raise questions about the educational mission of college sports. The bill includes no response to these objections beyond its tax and financial-aid carve-outs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for athletes are concrete: real bargaining rights over compensation and safety, in a market the bill's own findings describe as producing more than $15 billion a year [S2]. The costs fall on schools and conferences, and the strongest honest objection is that union-negotiated pay could squeeze non-revenue sports and small programs. The bill partially answers concerns about athletes' finances by protecting scholarship tax treatment and federal aid eligibility [S2]. It does not answer the budget concerns of smaller programs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025 [S4].

narrative.text: Representative Jamaal Bowman introduced the bill on December 6, 2023, joined by nine Democratic cosponsors including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ayanna Pressley-era progressives such as Rashida Tlaib and Ilhan Omar, and Emanuel Cleaver [S2].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, the committee with jurisdiction over labor law amendments [S4].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The NCAA's member institutions and athletic conferences, which keep setting athlete compensation and conditions without collective bargaining. College athletes remain without federal union rights.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: NCAA member schools and athletic conferences

for.name: Rep. Jamaal Bowman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the College Athlete Right to Organize Act and recruited nine cosponsors.

for.name: House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: 9 cosponsors, all Democrats (including Cleaver, Frost, Ocasio-Cortez, Omar, Ramirez, Thanedar, Tlaib, Lee of Pennsylvania, and Johnson of Georgia)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction; no further recorded action.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; no committee action of any kind was recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with a Republican-run committee, the bill never advanced past referral [S3][S4].

industries.note: Schools would become employers under labor law and would have to bargain over scholarships-as-pay and athlete conditions instead of setting terms unilaterally. Their interest in keeping the current system runs against the athletes' interest in bargaining rights [S2].

industries.industry: Athletic conferences (e.g., the SEC, Big Ten, ACC)
industries.note: The bill makes conferences multiemployer bargaining units, so league-wide rules on compensation and conditions could only be set through negotiation with athlete unions. Conferences currently set these rules without athlete input [S2].

The bill carves the NCAA out of the definition of a bargaining counterparty, so the association that governs eligibility and many of the rules athletes live under would not sit at the bargaining table even as its member schools gained new obligations [S2].
